A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeFT research, with matching algorithms, workloads, and core results. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original latency and IO measurements for few-shot prompting, multi-step reasoning, and speculative decoding, together with splitting-strategy and tree-width analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains the original experiments and adds numerical accuracy checks, GPU profiling, and experiments varying splitting strategies, models, hardware, prompt lengths, and chunk sizes.

M1.justification: V3 introduces DeFT-Node-Chunk, which subdivides individual nodes into KV blocks while retaining node-wise grouping (Section 3.3). This is a limited procedural addition. DeFT-Flatten's existing flattening, masking, and reduction procedure remains unchanged; Algorithms 1–4 are identical apart from formatting.

E1.justification: Both versions use APPS, the same four GoT-derived reasoning tasks, and Medusa-derived speculative decoding traces. The added experiments vary models, hardware, prompt padding, and metrics within these workloads, without introducing an identifiable new dataset or task.

E2.justification: V3 adds DeFT-Node-Chunk to evaluated comparisons and Hugging Face vanilla attention as the numerical reference in Table 15. Flash-Decoding, Tree Attention-Medusa, and Radix Attention remain the main external comparators. DeFT-Node's end-to-end latency and IO comparison rows disappear, although its attention comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain, but v3 adds CodeLlama-7B/34B, MHA/GQA comparisons, RTX 4090 experiments, sorting prompts padded to 5K–10K tokens, and chunk-size sweeps from 128 to 1024. New protocols measure GPU utilization and attention/PPL agreement, substantially broadening evaluation beyond the original latency and IO measurements.

E4.justification: V3 adds Node-Chunk ablations, GPU utilization profiling, numerical accuracy checks, and sensitivity studies covering prompt length, model size, architecture, GPU, and chunk size (Tables 6–8, 14–15, 18–21; Figure 15). The earlier topology and tree-width analyses remain. V2's Figure 13, containing four reasoning-task latency breakdowns, is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained node-length standard deviation describes tree structure. V3's new attention and PPL errors measure numerical agreement, rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: The main DeFT-Flatten latency and IO values are retained across v2 Tables 7/11/12 and v3 Tables 16/5/17. V3 adds extensive accuracy, utilization, Node-Chunk, and configuration-dependent results. DeFT-Node's b=30 attention latency changes from 11.41 to 10.62 seconds, and previously unsupported cases receive results. Its end-to-end/IO rows and the four-task latency breakdowns are removed.

T1.justification: V2's explicit decoding-tree and tree-attention definitions are omitted. The IO analysis moves from Section 3.4 to Appendix A.5 and gains Radix Attention and Node-Chunk entries, including the latter's sum-of-ceilings group-count formula. The segmented-softmax equation restates the existing merging identity rather than establishing a new theorem.

C1.justification: The central IO-reduction claims and headline 2.52×/3.82× speedups remain. V3 centers the contribution on DeFT-Flatten, explicitly adds comparison of three splitting strategies, and extends the conclusion to claim effectiveness across LLM models and GPU architectures. These are bounded extensions of the original contribution.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands interpretation: Node-Chunk's weakness with many small nodes, chunk-size tradeoffs between query IO and GPU scheduling, reduced gains when larger models increase FFN overhead, and floating-point explanations for numerical discrepancies. The dedicated limitations paragraph disappears, but the substantive qualification about limited benefits for small trees remains in Section 4.3.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses a default KV chunk size of 128 and NVIDIA Nsight Compute as the profiling tool, and specifies hardware, model, and measurement details for added experiments. The default-size disclosure does not establish a change to earlier experiments. Existing system descriptions and pseudocode are largely retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references to Quest and NVIDIA Nsight Compute documentation and refines descriptions of baseline partitioning and load balancing. The principal positioning against Flash-Decoding, Medusa, SpecInfer, SGLang, and concurrent prefix-sharing methods remains. The switch to author-year citations is a presentation change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method exposition are substantially rewritten around prefix-aware and balanced QKV partitioning. Segmented attention becomes introductory material, the IO analysis moves to the appendix, and the final section becomes a conclusion. This reorganizes the argument substantially beyond merely appending experiments.

P2.justification: V3 redesigns the overview and partitioning diagrams, expands and transposes Table 2, and adds a supplementary tree-attention diagram. End-to-end results move into the main text while attention results move to the appendix. Numerous analytical tables and a chunk-size plot are added, and the four-panel reasoning latency breakdown is removed.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation that was concentrated on latency and IO in v2. Numerical fidelity checks, direct GPU utilization measurements, the Node-Chunk comparison, and broader model/hardware experiments provide stronger evidence for correctness, the proposed mechanism, and applicability boundaries. The rewritten explanation also makes partitioning choices easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed reasoning-task latency breakdowns; the improvement comes from stronger support for retained results, rather than higher headline performance.
